A class library is a toolbox another application can reuse. It normally has no Main method and produces a DLL rather than its own user interface.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Two projects, one shared rule

The root StudyLab.csproj is the console app. SharedRules/SharedRules.csproj is a separate class library. ProjectReference links them. Open the root project in Visual Studio; the reference should restore/build with it. The root excludes SharedRules source from its own compilation so the same types are not compiled twice. 

dotnet add StudyLab.csproj reference SharedRules/SharedRules.csproj

The supplied project already includes that reference. MarkRules.IsPass(70) returns true. Keep dependencies and visibility minimal: public exposes a reusable contract, internal hides implementation details.

When to share code

Good candidates include validation rules, calculations and domain models shared by API, MVC and desktop applications. Avoid making a library depend on a specific window or controller. Package versioning matters when distributing a library through NuGet. Target a framework compatible with every consuming application; net10.0 does not run in a .NET8 consumer just because both use C#.

What is a practical benefit of one shared pass rule?

Worked answer

Fix the rule in one place and test it once, then rebuild/update the consuming applications.

Why not place database passwords inside the DLL?

Worked answer

Compiled assemblies can be inspected. Secrets belong in runtime configuration with controlled access.
